topicTitle: Dynamic Web Pages: Modifying Content & Attributes

lessons.title: Creating & Appending Elements (createElement, append, appendChild)
lessons.description: Build new HTML elements with JavaScript and add them to the page dynamically.

sections.heading: Creating elements
paragraphs: JavaScript can create brand-new HTML elements using document.createElement(). The element exists in memory but isn't on the page yet — you must attach it to a parent node to make it visible.
list: parent.appendChild(child) — adds element at the end of parent
parent.append(child) — adds element and can accept strings too
parent.prepend(child) — adds element at the beginning of parent

codeExamples.heading: Creating and appending elements
explanation: createElement creates the element but doesn't add it anywhere yet.
appendChild inserts at the end of the parent.
append is more flexible — it accepts strings and multiple arguments.

practice.task: Write JavaScript that creates a new <li> element with the text "Hello" and appends it to an existing <ul>.

keyTakeaways: createElement() creates an element in memory, not on the page.
appendChild() and append() add elements to a parent node.
prepend() adds at the beginning instead of the end.
You must set text, classes and attributes before appending for efficiency.
lessons.challenge: Write a function that creates 5 list items dynamically, each with a different number as text, and appends them all to a <ul>.

lessons.title: Modifying Text Safely with textContent (vs innerHTML Risks)
lessons.description: Update element text with textContent for safety, and understand why innerHTML can be dangerous.

sections.heading: textContent — safe text replacement
paragraphs: textContent sets or reads the plain text inside an element. It automatically escapes HTML, so user input can never accidentally become executable markup.
list: element.textContent = "Hello" — sets plain text, escaping any HTML
element.textContent — reads all text including hidden elements
Safe for user-generated content — no XSS risk

sections.heading: innerHTML — powerful but risky
paragraphs: innerHTML lets you set raw HTML inside an element. It's useful for inserting formatted content but dangerous when used with untrusted input — malicious scripts can slip in.
list: Never use innerHTML with user input unless you sanitize it first
textContent is almost always the safer choice

codeExamples.heading: textContent vs innerHTML
explanation: textContent escapes everything — angle brackets appear as literal text.
innerHTML parses and renders HTML — useful for formatted content.
User input via innerHTML can execute malicious scripts (XSS attacks).
Always use textContent unless you specifically need to render HTML.

practice.task: Create an element and set its content using textContent with HTML tags in the string. Observe that the tags appear as plain text. Then use innerHTML to see the difference.

keyTakeaways: textContent is safe — it escapes HTML automatically.
innerHTML renders raw HTML — useful but risky with untrusted data.
Always prefer textContent for user-generated content to prevent XSS.
Use innerHTML only when you need to insert formatted HTML from trusted sources.
lessons.challenge: Build a simple input form that takes a username and displays it on the page using textContent to ensure no HTML injection is possible.

lessons.title: Dynamic Styling: Class Manipulation via classList (add, remove, toggle)
lessons.description: Add, remove and toggle CSS classes on elements without touching the style attribute directly.

sections.heading: The classList API
paragraphs: Rather than setting element.className (which replaces all classes), use the classList property to add, remove or toggle individual classes. It's safer and more convenient.
list: classList.toggle("class") — adds if missing, removes if present

codeExamples.heading: Using classList methods
explanation: add() can take multiple class names at once.
toggle() is perfect for click handlers — it flips the class state.
contains() checks if a class is present — useful for conditional logic.
Using classList keeps your styles in CSS and your behavior in JavaScript.

practice.task: Create a button that toggles a .dark-mode class on the body when clicked. Define .dark-mode in your CSS to change the background and text colors.
hints: The toggle approach means one click enables it, another click disables it.

keyTakeaways: classList.add(), .remove() and .toggle() manage individual classes safely.
classList.toggle() is ideal for click-based toggling like dark mode.
Keep styling in CSS and use JavaScript to toggle classes — separation of concerns.
Avoid setting className directly — it replaces all classes instead of modifying individual ones.
lessons.challenge: Build a theme switcher with 3 themes (light, dark, ocean). Use classList to apply the selected theme to the body and save the preference with localStorage.

lessons.title: Reading & Writing HTML Attributes (getAttribute, setAttribute, dataset)
lessons.description: Access and modify element attributes and use data-* attributes for custom metadata.

sections.heading: Working with attributes
paragraphs: Elements have attributes like id, class, href and src. JavaScript can read and write any attribute using getAttribute() and setAttribute().
list: setAttribute("name", value) — sets or creates an attribute

sections.heading: Custom data attributes
paragraphs: HTML5 lets you store custom data on elements using data-* attributes. JavaScript accesses them through the dataset property.

codeExamples.heading: Attribute and dataset manipulation
explanation: getAttribute reads the current value — always prefer it over direct property access.
setAttribute can create new attributes that don't exist yet.

practice.task: Create an <a> tag with a data-url attribute. Use JavaScript to read the data attribute and update the href to match it.

keyTakeaways: getAttribute() and setAttribute() read and write any HTML attribute.
data-* attributes store custom data — access via element.dataset.
Hyphenated data attributes convert to camelCase in JavaScript (e.g., data-user-id becomes userId).
Use removeAttribute() to clean up attributes you no longer need.
lessons.challenge: Build a product card that stores price and category as data attributes. Write JavaScript that reads these and displays them in a summary div below the card.

lessons.title: Removing DOM Nodes (remove, removeChild)
lessons.description: Delete elements from the page cleanly using remove() and removeChild().

sections.heading: Removing elements
paragraphs: Removing elements from the DOM is as simple as adding them. The .remove() method deletes an element directly, while removeChild() removes a specific child from a parent.
list: Removed elements are garbage collected if no references remain
You can save a reference before removing to re-insert elsewhere

codeExamples.heading: Removing elements from the DOM
explanation: .remove() is the simplest — just call it on the element.
removeChild() returns the removed node, which you can re-insert elsewhere.
When removing multiple children, always remove from the front to avoid index shifting issues.

practice.task: Write JavaScript that removes the last item from a list each time a button is clicked, until the list is empty.
hints: Use list.lastChild or list.lastElementChild to get the last item.
Call .remove() on it inside a click handler.

keyTakeaways: .remove() is the cleanest way to delete an element from the DOM.
removeChild() is useful when you need the parent reference or want the removed node back.
Removed elements are garbage collected if no other references point to them.
When removing multiple children, remove from the front or collect all references first.
lessons.challenge: Build a to-do list where each item has a delete button. Clicking the delete button should remove that specific item from the DOM.
